questions.q: Per this lesson, what's the key difference between duration and CPU time?
options: Duration is wall-clock elapsed time and includes time spent waiting; CPU time is only the time the processor actually spent executing
They always measure exactly the same thing
CPU time includes network latency but duration does not
Duration only applies to stored procedures, not ad hoc queries
questions.explain: Duration can include lock waits, I/O waits, or parallel thread waits that CPU time excludes entirely, which is why the two can disagree sharply.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call logical reads the most stable of the three metrics?
options: For the same plan against the same data, logical reads barely change run to run, unlike duration which can swing with server load
Logical reads is measured in seconds, making it directly comparable to CPU time
Logical reads always equals duration for a well-tuned query
SQL Server never actually reports logical reads accurately
questions.explain: Duration depends on whatever else is happening on the server at that moment; logical reads reflects the actual work the plan does against the data, which is far more consistent.

questions.q: A query shows 8 seconds of duration but only 200 milliseconds of CPU time. What does this gap suggest, per the lesson?
options: The query is spending most of its time waiting on something (a lock, I/O, etc.), not computing — so indexing or rewriting the query likely won't help
The query is CPU-bound and needs a better index immediately
The measurement is invalid and should be discarded
The server has too much available CPU capacity
questions.explain: A large duration-vs-CPU gap points to a waiting problem, which needs wait-based diagnosis, not query rewriting or indexing.

questions.q: What command turns on reporting of CPU time, elapsed time, and logical reads for a query run in SSMS?
options: SET STATISTICS TIME, IO ON
SET NOCOUNT ON
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED
DBCC FREEPROCCACHE
questions.explain: SET STATISTICS TIME ON and SET STATISTICS IO ON report CPU/elapsed time and page read counts in the Messages pane for each statement executed.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why isn't "the database is slow" a diagnosis?
options: It's a symptom report — it has to be turned into a specific, measured target (e.g., duration, CPU time, or logical reads for a specific query) before you can act on it
Because databases are never actually slow, only applications are
Because SQL Server does not expose any way to measure query performance
Because tuning should always start with a full server reboot
questions.explain: A vague complaint gives you nothing to measure before/after; naming the specific metric and its current value is what makes a problem actionable.
